newsitem.title: UK: Unocal to update Turkmen president on oil project.
newsitem.headline: Unocal to update Turkmen president on oil project.

text.p: A team of senior executives from U.S. oil company Unocal left London on Friday for Turkmenistan to update President Saparmurat Niyazov on two major pipeline projects linking the central Asian republic with Pakistan.

The team, led by Marty Miller, vice president with responsibility for new ventures in the Middle East and Central Asia, has prepared a Project Definition Report, due by October 21 but prepared early, outlining the current status of the projects.
Unocal is working on the projects with Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil Company.

The two projects, the Central Asian Oil Pipeline Project (CAOPP) and the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan Gas Pipeline Project, valued at $2.5 billion and $2 billion respectively, both involve the construction of new links from Turkmenistan to Pakistan.
"When we started in central Asia five or six years ago, what we saw was an incredible oil and gas resource province but with no pipelines," Miller told Reuters.
"We decided that if we're to be in the area, we must be pro-active and indeed a leader at exporting."
The projects are ambitious, as both involve transiting war-torn Afghanistan before terminating in Pakistan. But Unocal is confident that this problem can be overcome.
"There are several factions controlling parts of Afghanistan," said Chris Taggart, executive vice president in charge of the gas pipeline project.
"Our policy is to be absolutely politically neutral. But we have opened dialogues with the leaders of all the factions. The project has written support from the leaders of all the factions.
"All have agreed separately on the benefits of the project, and have also agreed that they must form a single entity to allow its development.
"We don't think a pipeline can bring peace to a country, but we do think it can give common ground for forming a council to represent them on a single subject."
He said Unocal was committed to making non-cash bonus payments in the form of humanitarian aid on the successful completion of a council in Afghanistan to supervise the project.

If the project goes ahead, the gas line will connect the Dauletabad gas field in southern Turkmenistan with Multan on Pakistan's existing gas grid. Multan is well placed for a future extension into India. The line be between 870 and 890 miles long, and will have a capacity of 20 billion cubic metres a year (around two billion cubic feet per day)
Dauletabad currently produces two bcfpd of gas, and the Turkmen government has signed an agreement with Unocal making the field's output available for export through the line.
Taggart said independent surveys have put the field's reserves at 20 trillion cubic feet.
"There is a credible and growing gas market in Pakistan, and the market in India is huge," he added.
The CAOPP oil project is also ambitious, involving the construction of entirely new loading facilities offshore Pakistan.

Bob Todor, executive vice president responsible for the CAOPP, said the line will start in Chardzhou, a refining centre in central Turkmenistan, and run due south through Afghanistan to the coast of Pakistan, a distance of 1,000 miles.
"There is growing oil supply coming from the Caspian republics and central Asia, especially Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan," he said.
"And Chardzhou is already connected to the western Siberian oilfields by existing pipelines. Supply is growing very fast and needs a way out."
Todor said the main benefit of CAOPP's one million barrels per day line was that it would offer easy access to the fast growing markets of east Asia.

"What we really offer is that Asian market when all other routes from the area go to Europe," he said. The offshore loading facilities in Pakistan will allow VLCCs (very large crude carriers) to load, an advantage which neither Black Sea nor Baltic ports can offer.
The team said finance will be difficult to raise.
"We think both projects will not be financeable by project finance," said Miller. "We don't believe they will be more than 50 percent financed. The rest will have to come from investor equity."
He said they were focusing on the World Bank, the Asia Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
"If the Afghans stop fighting, the World Bank is ready to invest in the country to reinforce the peace," he added.
Taggart said the project will take three years "from the start of financial closing to physical start up," but when this three-year period starts will largely depend on the situation in Afghanistan.
